authorities.name: Gambling Act 2005, s.42
authorities.date_note: Enactment year. The text verified this session is the current in-force version.
authorities.proposition: A person commits an offence if he cheats at gambling, or does anything for the purpose of enabling or assisting another person to cheat at gambling (s.42(1)). Without prejudice to the generality of that provision, cheating may in particular consist of actual or attempted deception or interference with the process by which gambling is conducted, or with the game/race/event to which the gambling relates (s.42(3)) - a non-exhaustive, deliberately open-textured definition.
authorities.verification_note: Fetched live and directly this session, on two independent passes, word-for-word consistent both times.

authorities.name: Ivey v Genting Casinos (UK) Ltd t/a Crockfords
authorities.judge_or_panel: Lord Neuberger, Lady Hale, Lord Kerr, Lord Hughes (leading judgment), Lord Thomas
authorities.proposition: Section 42's concept of cheating does not require proof of a separate legal element of dishonesty - the section's open-textured wording leaves what counts as cheating to depend on the nature and rules of the particular game, assessed objectively by the court rather than by the defendant's own belief about whether the conduct was legitimate. Applying that construction, a professional gambler's 'edge-sorting' technique - manipulating an unwitting croupier into sorting high-value cards in a game of pure chance - was cheating, even though he genuinely and honestly believed it was legitimate advantage play. The appeal against the casino's refusal to pay his winnings was dismissed. The case is a real civil dispute (a professional gambler's multi-million-pound claim for withheld winnings) in which s.42's meaning was directly determinative.
authorities.verification_note: This session's own attempt to independently re-fetch and decode the official Supreme Court PDF judgment failed - the tool explicitly reported it could not render the compressed PDF content, on both the judgment PDF itself and a fetch of the case's press-summary page. The outcome (appeal dismissed) and the core holding (dishonesty is not a required separate element of s.42 cheating; an objective standard applies) were instead independently corroborated via a live Wikipedia fetch this session, consistent with the researching agent's account.
